The system monitor service

monitord runs once on every MixOS host, as its own unprivileged user. It samples the system every second, keeps history, and answers questions about the host on the Bus. It only reads. The reasons are in the monitord decision.

Monitor, the task manager window, draws what monitord serves. Agents and scripts ask it directly.

Asking it

On the Bus, the service is monitord. Any node's monitord is reachable over the mesh as monitord.<node>.bus:

send monitord monitord.snapshot
print($reply.cpu.busy)

send monitord.alpha.bus monitord.processes sort=memory limit=5

Every command is a query: it changes nothing. A refusal comes back with rc 10 and a body whose status says why: bad_request, not_found, failed or busy. An unknown command gets the refusal every component gives: error_code UNKNOWN_COMMAND, with message and command.

CommandBodyReturns
monitord.status—Version, uptime, sample interval, whether the process sampler is running, and the history database's size and retention
monitord.snapshot—The system now (below)
monitord.processessort, reverse, limit, filter, user, tree, kernel_threadsThe process table
monitord.processpidOne process in full
monitord.series—The history series held: live and stored
monitord.connectionslimit, sort, state, portLive TCP peers, throughput, RTT, retransmits and owning user
monitord.historyseries, from or since, to, max_pointsPoints for each series

Unknown body fields are refused, so a typo is an error, not a silent default.

monitord.snapshot

Rates and percentages are over the last sample interval (interval_s). Sizes are bytes; rates are per second.

  • host, ts (Unix seconds), uptime_s, boot_time.
  • cpu: model, cores, and busy, user, system, iowait, steal in percent; per_core, a list of the same per CPU with mhz; context_switches_ps, forks_ps.
  • memory: total, available, used (total - available), free, cached, buffers, shared, dirty. swap: total, used, free.
  • load: one, five, fifteen, runnable, tasks.
  • pressure: for cpu, memory and io, the share of time tasks stalled (some, and full where the kernel reports it), each as avg10, avg60, avg300. Absent on kernels without PSI.
  • tasks: total, running, blocked.
  • disks: each whole disk with model, rotational, read_bps, write_bps, reads_ps, writes_ps and busy (percent of the interval with I/O in flight). Loop and RAM devices are left out.
  • filesystems: each real filesystem once per device, with mount, device, kind, total, used, available.
  • net: each interface but loopback, with state, physical, speed_mbps, rx_bps, tx_bps and the running totals.
  • tcp: in_segs, out_segs, retrans_segs, in_errs, active_opens, passive_opens, out_rsts, estab_resets, listen_overflows and listen_drops, all events per second over interval_s; established is the current established/close-wait gauge (CurrEstab). sockstat holds TCP inuse, orphan, tw, alloc counts and mem (kernel buffer pages), exactly as /proc/net/sockstat reports them. Its inuse is IPv4 only; the other fields are kernel-wide TCP counters. sockstat6 reports /proc/net/sockstat6's TCP6 fields separately (normally only IPv6 inuse; absent fields are null). Add the two inuse values for the IPv4 + IPv6 total. These and /proc/net/snmp (Tcp) and /proc/net/netstat (TcpExt) are read without a connection scan.

A value monitord can't know is null, never zero. Counter resets or wrap give a null rate for that interval, as do counters without a previous sample. The next interval resumes normally.

monitord.connections

{"limit":20,"sort":"throughput","state":"established","port":443}

Shows the host's peers, like ss. An unprivileged NETLINK_SOCK_DIAG inet_diag dump covers IPv4 and IPv6 full sockets and requests INET_DIAG_INFO (tcp_info). No new crate or capability is needed: the reader uses the existing libc dependency and Linux UAPI byte layouts. TIME_WAIT and NEW_SYN_RECV are excluded from the request: neither carries tcp_info, so neither consumes the 65,536-socket cap. TIME_WAIT totals remain available in tcp.sockstat.tw.

  • limit defaults to 20 and is clamped to 1–1000.
  • sort: throughput (rx + tx, default), rx, tx, rtt or retransmits, largest first; ties use the socket cookie. Throughput puts every measured rate, including zero, before unavailable rates. Listening sockets rank last and only fill spare places after non-listening sockets; a full top 20 with traffic contains no listeners. An explicit state: "listen" query still returns listeners.
  • state: optional kernel state name: established, syn-sent, syn-recv, fin-wait-1, fin-wait-2, time-wait, close, close-wait, last-ack, listen, closing or new-syn-recv. time-wait and new-syn-recv remain accepted filters for compatibility but return no rows, because those states are excluded from the dump.
  • port: optional port number matching either endpoint.

The reply has ts, total (matching sockets), count and rows. Each row has cookie (the two idiag_cookie words), local, remote (IP addresses), local_port, remote_port, ifindex, state, rx_bps, tx_bps, rtt_us, retransmits (lifetime tcpi_total_retrans), uid and user. The uid is idiag_uid; the name comes from readable /etc/passwd, otherwise its numeric uid. Connections and processes share one users cache, refreshed after 60 s. There is no process attribution. IPv6 addresses stay unbracketed in JSON; the UI brackets peer endpoints.

Each request holds a separate sampler on for 30 s. A cold request takes two dumps one configured sample interval apart (1 s by default); background ticks skip that pair so its baseline cannot be replaced. Rates are bytes_received and bytes_acked deltas divided by elapsed monotonic time, matched by cookie. New sockets, resets and unavailable tcp_info fields have null rates. Closed sockets disappear. No summed host TCP byte rate is reported because it would miss bytes from closing sockets.

Nothing per connection is stored in history. The sampler drops idle state after its hold expires, caps each dump at 65,536 sockets, each datagram at 64 KiB and the complete dump at 2 s, including retries for send or receive backpressure. Oversized or interrupted dumps fail explicitly rather than showing a misleading partial top list.

Privacy: peer addresses, ports and users are open to Bus readers, including readers on the mesh, just as process command lines are. Watching a remote node shows that host's peers. No payloads are read or retained. monitord.status.connection_sampler reports activity, cached row count and the latest sampling error.

monitord.processes

{"sort":"cpu", "limit":100, "filter":"firefox", "user":"alice", "tree":false}
  • sort is cpu (the default), memory, io, pid, name or user. Numbers sort largest first and names A to Z; reverse flips it.
  • limit defaults to 100; 0 means every row.
  • filter matches the name or command line, ignoring case.
  • tree puts parents before children, siblings in sort order, each row with its depth. A filter keeps a match's ancestors, so the tree still joins up.
  • The kernel's own threads are left out unless kernel_threads is true.

The reply has total (rows that matched), count (rows returned) and rows. Each row has pid, ppid, name, cmdline, user, uid, state, cpu, memory (resident), virtual_memory, threads, nice, priority, started_at, read_bps, write_bps, unit (the systemd service or scope) and kernel_thread.

cpu is a share of the whole machine, as Task Manager shows it: one busy core of eight is 12.5.

The process table is sampled only while someone reads it. A call keeps the sampler running for 30 seconds. The first call after a quiet spell takes two scans 0.3 s apart, so it answers in about a third of a second.

monitord runs unprivileged, so another user's I/O counters, open files and working directory are unreadable to it. Those fields are null.

monitord.process

{"pid": 1234} returns the table's fields plus exe, cwd, the whole cmdline, cpu_time_s, memory_peak, swap, read_bytes, write_bytes, open_files, voluntary_switches, involuntary_switches, cgroup and children.

monitord.history

{"series":["cpu.busy","net.*"], "since":3600, "max_points":600}
  • series is one name or a list. A name ending in * matches a prefix: cpu.core.* is every core.
  • Give from (Unix seconds) or since (seconds back from to); the default is the last ten minutes. to defaults to now.
  • Each point is [time, average, minimum, maximum]. Points are merged into buckets of step_s seconds so a series has at most max_points (default 600).
  • tier says where the points came from:
TierResolutionKeptSeries
liveevery sample10 minutesall, per core included
minute1 minute7 dayssystem-wide
hour1 hour1 yearsystem-wide

The series are cpu.busy, cpu.user, cpu.system, cpu.iowait, cpu.steal, mem.used, mem.available, mem.cached, swap.used, load.1, load.5, load.15, psi.<cpu|memory|io>.<some|full>, disk.<name>.<read|write|busy> and net.<name>.<rx|tx>, plus, in memory only, cpu.core.<n>.busy and cpu.core.<n>.mhz.

TCP adds exactly these stored series to all three tiers (average, minimum, maximum): tcp.in_segs, tcp.out_segs, tcp.retrans_segs, tcp.in_errs, tcp.active_opens, tcp.passive_opens, tcp.out_rsts, tcp.estab_resets, tcp.listen_overflows, tcp.listen_drops (rates/s) and tcp.established (gauge). Sockstat counts appear only in the live snapshot. Retransmit percentages are computed by Monitor from the two rate series, never stored.

Reader references: the kernel's SNMP counter documentation and the Linux UAPI headers linux/inet_diag.h, linux/netlink.h and linux/tcp.h.

The summary topic

Every 5 seconds monitord publishes a small retained summary on monitord.summary: host, CPU busy and core count, memory, swap, load, total network and disk rates, the 10-second pressure figures and the task count. A mesh dashboard subscribes to it instead of polling every node.

The command line

The same binary works with no daemon running. It reads the kernel itself, so it answers on a node's console or over ssh either way:

monitord snapshot            the system now, sampled over half a second
monitord ps --sort memory    the process table (--tree, --user, --filter, --all)
monitord history cpu.busy --since 86400    stored history from the database
monitord signal 1234 TERM    send a signal, as you
monitord renice 1234 10      change a nice value, as you

--json prints what the matching command returns. signal and renice run as the person who typed them, and the kernel decides whether they may. No Bus command signals or renices anything: acting across users or nodes is hostd's job.

Running it

monitord.service runs <prefix>/bin/monitord serve as the user monitord, with no capabilities and a strict sandbox. The history database is /var/lib/monitord/history.db; it is a cache, and deleting it loses history and nothing else.

serve takes:

  • --interval-ms (default 1000);
  • --db PATH or --no-db;
  • --minute-days (default 7) and --hour-days (default 365);
  • --no-bus, to sample and record without joining the Bus.

When the broker is down, monitord keeps sampling and recording, and joins when it comes back.

Testing

cargo test -p monitord

The kernel readers take fixture text, and command tests use fixture /proc and /sys trees. Netlink encode/decode tests use captured, neutralised wire fixtures; a separate unprivileged test dumps its own loopback TCP sockets on the build worker. No test needs a broker.
